title: Hashing
summary: Hash tables turn a key into an array index with hashCode and a modulus, keep collisions in short chains, and resize to keep the load factor constant, giving Θ(1) expected operations. Exams trace inserts and resizes, judge hash functions, find equals/hashCode contract bugs and mutable-key traps, and ask you to pick the right data structure for a design.

blocks.text: If keys were small integers we could use them as array indices (a “DataIndexedArray”): Θ(1) everything, but memory proportional to the key range. Hashing compresses any key into a small index range.
A function from keys to ints (Java: hashCode()). It must be deterministic and consistent with equals.
Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), M) for M buckets. floorMod (not %) keeps negative hash codes in range: floorMod(−3, 8) = 5 while −3 % 8 = −3.
Two keys landing in the same bucket. Unavoidable (pigeonhole: infinitely many keys, M buckets).
Math.abs(h) % M is not safe either: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still Integer.MIN_VALUE (negative), and the String "polygenelubricants" actually has hash code Integer.MIN_VALUE.

blocks.name: String.hashCode
blocks.text: For s of length n: s[0]·31^(n−1) + s[1]·31^(n−2) + ⋯ + s[n−1], computed with int overflow. Computed by the loop h = 31·h + c.

blocks.title: Compute String hash codes
steps: "Aa" = 65·31 + 97 = 2112; "BB" = 66·31 + 66 = 2112: a collision between different strings.

items: Integer.hashCode(x) = x (so −7 hashes to −7). Boolean: true → 1231. Long: high and low 32 bits XORed (1L << 32 hashes to 1).
Default Object.hashCode is identity-based: two equal objects of a class that overrides equals but not hashCode almost surely hash differently.

blocks.name: Good hash codes
blocks.text: Spread keys evenly over all ints and use every part of the key that equals uses. Multiplying by a prime like 31 before adding the next component makes order matter and avoids systematic collisions.

blocks.title: Good vs bad hashCode for points
blocks.prompt: Points (x, y) with 0 ≤ x, y < 100 (10,000 points). Compare hashCode = x + y with hashCode = 31x + y.
steps: x + y takes only 199 distinct values (0 … 198); about 50 points share each value on average, and resizing can never separate keys with equal hash codes.
31x + y takes 3169 distinct values here (31x + y collides only when y differs by a multiple of 31 with x adjusted), far better; a full-range mixing hash would give 10,000.
Return 0 for every key: one bucket holds everything → Θ(N) per operation.

blocks.text: Keep an array of M buckets, each a list. With N items the average chain length is the load factor α = N/M. Resize (double M and rehash every item) whenever α exceeds a constant threshold, so chains stay Θ(1) long on average.
α = N / M  ·  resize when α > threshold  ·  new index = floorMod(hashCode, newM)

blocks.title: Insert and resize trace
blocks.prompt: M = 4, keys are Integers (hashCode = value), new items go to the end of their chain, and after an insert, if N/M > 1, M doubles and items are rehashed by scanning buckets 0, 1, … in order. Insert 5, 28, 19, 15, 20, 33, 12, 17, 10, −3.
steps: 20 → bucket 0 ([28, 20]); N = 5 > 4 → resize to 8. Rehash in scan order: 28 → 4, 20 → 4, 5 → 5, 19 → 3, 15 → 7.

blocks.text: Open addressing (linear probing) is the alternative: store items directly in the array and, on collision, try the next slot. It needs α < 1 and deletion is tricky; Java’s HashMap uses chaining.

lesson.title: The equals/hashCode contract and mutable keys

blocks.name: Contract
blocks.text: a.equals(b) ⇒ a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). A HashMap first jumps to the bucket of hashCode, then searches it with equals. If equal keys can hash differently, lookups search the wrong bucket.

blocks.title: Contract bugs
blocks.prompt: For each class, say what happens in a HashSet: (a) equals compares names, hashCode returns name.length() + age. (b) equals compares id, hashCode returns 42. (c) equals compares (x, y), hashCode inherited from Object.
steps: (a) Broken: two equal objects (same name) with different ages hash differently → duplicates stored, contains fails.
(b) Legal (equal ⇒ equal hash) but terrible: every key collides → Θ(N) operations.
(c) Broken: identity hash codes differ for equal points → duplicates, failed lookups.

blocks.title: Mutating a key
blocks.prompt: A List<Integer> key = [1, 2] is put into a HashSet, then key.add(3). What do contains(key) and contains(List.of(1, 2)) return?
steps: The list was stored in the bucket for hash of [1, 2].
After mutation its hash is that of [1, 2, 3]: contains(key) looks in a different bucket (almost surely) → false.
contains(List.of(1, 2)) looks in the right bucket, but the stored object is now [1, 2, 3], not equal → false. The entry is stranded but still counted in size.

blocks.title: Pick structures for a design
blocks.prompt: Support insert(x), remove(x) and getRandom() (uniformly random stored element), each in Θ(1) expected.
steps: A hash set alone can’t pick a uniformly random element in Θ(1). An ArrayList can (random index), but removal is Θ(N).
Combine: ArrayList a of elements + HashMap pos from element to its index in a.
remove(x): i = pos.get(x); move the last element into slot i (update its pos), remove the last slot, delete x from pos. All Θ(1).
Trace: insert 10, 20, 30, 40; remove 20 → 40 moves into index 1: a = [10, 40, 30], pos = {10: 0, 40: 1, 30: 2}.

cards.front: How does Java turn a hashCode into a bucket index?

back.text: Math.floorMod(hashCode, M) (or a bit mask when M is a power of 2).
Hash codes can be negative; % would give a negative index.
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is negative.
Σ s[i]·31^(n−1−i), with int overflow; loop h = 31h + c.
Both 2112: different strings can collide.
x itself.
α = N/M, the average chain length.
To keep α bounded so chains are Θ(1) long on average.

cards.front: Cost of one resize? Amortized put cost?

back.text: Θ(N) for the resize; Θ(1) amortized (with doubling).

cards.front: Worst case of a hash table operation?

back.text: Θ(N): all keys in one bucket (bad hashCode or adversarial keys).

cards.front: Can resizing fix a hashCode that returns a constant?

back.text: No: equal hash codes always share a bucket regardless of M.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

cards.front: Is hashCode returning 42 for everything legal?

back.text: Legal (satisfies the contract) but makes every operation Θ(N).

cards.front: What goes wrong when a key is mutated inside a HashMap?

back.text: It sits in the bucket of its old hash; lookups by the new or old value fail.
Chaining: lists per bucket, α can exceed 1. Probing: items in the array itself, try next slot on collision, needs α < 1.
HashMap Θ(1) expected, no order. TreeMap Θ(log N), sorted keys, floor/ceiling/range.

cards.front: Why does 31 appear in hash codes?

back.text: An odd prime multiplier that spreads values and makes the order of components matter.

cards.front: Iterating over a hash table costs?

back.text: Θ(N + M).

cards.front: Data structure for insert, remove, getRandom in Θ(1)?

back.text: ArrayList + HashMap from element to index; remove by swapping with the last element.
HashMap from key to node of a doubly linked list ordered by recency: Θ(1) get/put/evict.
Yes: List.of(1, 2) and List.of(2, 1) hash to 994 and 1024.

hard.title: LRU cache

prompt.text: Design an LRU cache with capacity k supporting get(key) and put(key, value) in Θ(1) expected; when full, put evicts the least recently used key (get and put both count as uses). Describe the structure and trace capacity 3: put 1, put 2, put 3, get 1, put 4, get 2, get 3, put 5.

hard.answer: HashMap key → DLL node + DLL in recency order; final keys (old → new) 4, 3, 5

solution.text: A doubly linked list (with sentinel) holds entries from least to most recently used; a HashMap maps each key to its node.

get: look up the node, unlink it and move it to the most-recent end (Θ(1) with prev/next pointers). put: if present update and move; else create a node at the recent end, and if size > k remove the node at the old end and delete its key from the map.
Trace: [1], [1 2], [1 2 3]; get 1 → [2 3 1]; put 4 → evict 2 → [3 1 4]; get 2 → miss; get 3 → [1 4 3]; put 5 → evict 1 → [4 3 5]. Verified with a reference implementation.

hard.title: Insert, remove, getRandom in Θ(1)

prompt.text: Implement a set with insert(x), remove(x), getRandom() all Θ(1) expected (getRandom returns each stored element with equal probability). Write remove.

hard.answer: ArrayList + HashMap(element → index); swap with last on remove

solution.text: The order of the last two pos updates matters when x is the last element: putting last → i first and then removing x leaves the map correct.
After inserting 10, 20, 30, 40 and removing 20: a = [10, 40, 30], pos = {10: 0, 30: 2, 40: 1}; remove(99) returns false (verified).

hard.title: Negative hash codes and abs

prompt.text: A student computes bucket indices as Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % M. (a) Find a String key for which this crashes when M = 10, and give the index it computes. (b) Why does M = 8 hide the bug? (c) Fix it.

hard.answer: "polygenelubricants" (hash Integer.MIN_VALUE) gives index −8; with M = 8 the result is 0; use Math.floorMod

solution.text: (a) "polygenelubricants".hashCode() is Integer.MIN_VALUE = −2147483648 (verified). Math.abs of it overflows back to −2147483648, and −2147483648 % 10 = −8 → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
(b) −2147483648 = −2³¹ is divisible by 8, so % 8 gives 0, a valid index — the bug only appears for moduli that don’t divide 2³¹.
(c) Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), M) always returns a value in [0, M).

hard.title: Resize trace with a different threshold

prompt.text: Separate chaining, M = 2 initially, new items appended to chains, resize (double, rehash in bucket-scan order) when N/M > 1.5 after an insert. Insert 7, 3, 12, 8, 21, 4. Give the final table.

hard.title: Which point hash scales?

prompt.text: N points (x, y) with 0 ≤ x, y < √N go into a chaining table with M = the smallest power of two > N, index floorMod(h, M). The total number of key comparisons for calling contains on every point was measured:
Explain each column and give the asymptotic total cost of N contains calls for the first three.

hard.answer: 31x+y and x+y: Θ(N^1.5); x·√N + y: Θ(N); x·65536 + y collapses because 65536 ≡ 0 mod M

solution.text: x + y has only 2√N − 1 distinct codes, so chains have length about √N: N lookups cost Θ(N·√N) = Θ(N^1.5). The column grows ×8 when N grows ×4, exactly the N^1.5 signature.
31x + y: codes 31x + y collide whenever y ≥ 31, so there are only about 32√N distinct codes: still Θ(N^1.5), just ~16× cheaper than x + y (ratios ≈ 7.0 and 7.4 per ×4 of N).
x·√N + y is a bijection onto 0 … N − 1 < M: every chain has length ≤ 1, total exactly N: Θ(N).

x·65536 + y: while M ≤ 65536, 65536·x ≡ 0 (mod M), so only y matters: √N codes, Θ(N^1.5) (×8 growth). At N = 160,000, M = 262,144 > 65536 and two bits of x survive, so it suddenly improves. Lesson: multipliers that share factors with M (powers of two with power-of-two M) destroy information. All counts verified by simulation.

hard.title: Design: first unique character, streaming

prompt.text: Characters arrive one at a time. After each, report the first character so far that has appeared exactly once (or none). Give a structure with Θ(1) amortized per character for an alphabet of any size.

hard.answer: HashMap counts + queue of candidates (lazy deletion)

solution.text: Keep a HashMap char → count and a queue of characters in arrival order (each enqueued on first appearance).
On arrival: increment the count (enqueue if it became 1). Then, while the queue’s front has count > 1, dequeue it. The front is the answer.

Each character is enqueued and dequeued at most once: Θ(1) amortized. (Alternative: LinkedHashMap of characters seen once, removing on the second sighting.) Stream a, b, a, c, b: answers a, a, b, b, c (verified).

keyFacts: Bucket = Math.floorMod(hashCode, M); never % or Math.abs (negatives, Integer.MIN_VALUE).
String hash: Σ s[i]·31^(n−1−i) with overflow; "Aa" and "BB" collide.
Load factor α = N/M; double M and rehash when α exceeds a threshold → Θ(1) expected (amortized) ops.
Worst case Θ(N) per op if hash codes collide; resizing cannot separate equal hash codes.
Contract: equals ⇒ equal hashCode. Constant hashCode is legal but Θ(N).
Never mutate a key’s hashCode fields while it is in a hash structure.
HashMap Θ(1) unordered vs TreeMap Θ(log N) ordered; combine structures for designs (LRU = HashMap + DLL).

parsons.title: Polynomial hashCode for an int sequence
parsons.goal: Return a hash code for a class holding int[] items, combining every element like String.hashCode does (so equal sequences hash equally and order matters).
